title: Validating Ground-Motion Simulations
subtitle: Ground-motion modeling
description: Comparing observed and simulated waveforms to evaluate Southern California Community Velocity Models.
details: Developed Python, Bash, and Slurm workflows for 3D spectral-element simulations using Salvus on high-performance computing clusters. The work compared multi-terabyte sets of observed and synthetic waveform data, using a novel goodness-of-fit approach to validate Southern California Community Velocity Models.
imageAlt: Observed and simulated basin/reference PSA amplification versus period in Los Angeles, San Fernando, San Gabriel, and Chino, with 95% event-bootstrap confidence intervals.
imageCaption: Basin amplification: observations compared with CVM-H and CVM-SI.
question: How well do 3D velocity models reproduce observed ground motion in Southern California’s sedimentary basins?
contribution: I developed Python, Bash, and Slurm workflows to run Salvus simulations on high-performance computing clusters and compare simulated waveforms with observations. The analysis evaluates model performance across stations and measures of ground motion.
significance: Comparisons with observations identify where a velocity model is useful and where it needs improvement. The basin-amplification figure provides one view of those differences across period and basin.

title: Generalized Differential Ambient Noise Tomography
subtitle: Tomographic method development
description: A mathematical framework for differential ambient noise tomographic imaging, evaluated with synthetic benchmarks.
details: Developed generalized differential ambient noise tomography, a mathematical framework for imaging subsurface structure from differential measurements of ambient seismic noise. Synthetic benchmarks were used to evaluate model recovery and compare the framework with traditional approaches.
imageAlt: Ambient noise from ocean microseisms reaches two seismic stations; cross-correlation of the station records reveals a time lag.
imageCaption: Ambient-noise cross-correlation between two seismic stations.
question: How can differential ambient noise measurements improve estimates of subsurface structure?
contribution: I developed the mathematical framework and evaluated it using synthetic benchmarks, connecting inverse-problem formulation with quantitative tests of model recovery.
significance: Synthetic tests allow the recovered structure to be compared with a known input model. They provide a controlled way to evaluate the method’s strengths and limitations before interpreting field observations.

title: Shallow Subsurface Imaging in the Nepal Himalaya
subtitle: Dense-array seismology
description: Applying ambient noise imaging to characterize shallow structure relevant to fluid flow and landslide processes.
details: As part of a multi-year NSF research project, I used ambient noise imaging to characterize shallow subsurface structure in the Nepal Himalaya. This work connects seismic imaging with questions about fluid flow and landslide processes in a multidisciplinary collaboration.
imageAlt: Shear-wave velocity cross-section along the ridgeline north of Melamchi, showing elevation, seismic stations, and labeled settlements.
imageCaption: Inverted shear-wave velocity profile along the Himalayan ridgeline.
question: What can dense seismic observations reveal about shallow structure in a steep mountain landscape?
contribution: I applied ambient noise imaging to characterize shallow subsurface structure and worked with collaborators to connect the seismic observations with hydrological and geomorphic questions.
significance: The velocity cross-section provides a spatial view of subsurface variability. Interpreting this structure alongside other observations helps investigate possible connections between the subsurface, fluid flow, and landsliding.

title: Locating Himalayan Microseismicity
subtitle: Earthquake catalog development
description: Combining machine learning–based phase picking, association, and relocation to locate small earthquakes.
details: Developed a workflow for locating small earthquakes in the Nepal Himalaya using machine learning–based seismic phase picking, association, and double-difference relocation.
imageAlt: Placeholder schematic of seismic phase picks and earthquake locations, not actual research data.
question: How can continuous seismic records be turned into a catalog of small earthquakes?
contribution: I combined phase picking, association, and relocation to turn waveform observations into earthquake locations. The workflow brings together seismic signal analysis and computational processing.
significance: An earthquake catalog provides a basis for studying the spatial distribution of seismicity. Interpreting individual events in relation to faults requires evaluating location uncertainty and the available geological constraints.
